title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 109
paragraphs: As time went on, however, the matter became known in the following way. Amestris, Xerxes's wife, had woven a mantle — large, of various workmanship, and a sight worth seeing — and she gave it to Xerxes. Greatly pleased, he put it on and went to Artaÿnte. Being greatly pleased with her too, he bade her ask whatever she wanted to be given in return for the favors she had granted him, for she would obtain, he said, whatever she asked. Since it was destined that she should perish miserably along with her whole house, she said to Xerxes: “Will you give me whatever I ask?” He, supposing she would ask anything rather than what she did, promised this and swore to it. Then when he had sworn, she boldly asked for the mantle. Xerxes tried every means of persuasion, not wanting to give it to her — and for no other reason than that he feared Amestris, lest by her (who even before this had some inkling of the truth) he should thus be caught out. He offered her cities and gold in any quantity, and an army that no one else should command except herself — this last being a thoroughly Persian gift. When, however, he could not persuade her, he gave her the mantle; and she, overjoyed by the gift, wore it and prided herself on it.
